tier_reason: tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks README summary table carries the cppcoro, concurrencpp, HPX and libcoro rows exactly as claimed; benchmark code is public (cpp/cppcoro/skynet.cpp, nqueens.cpp, fib.cpp, matmul.cpp and the matching cpp/concurrencpp, cpp/HPX, cpp/libcoro files, driven by build_and_bench_all.py) with Clang 21.1.7 Release (-O3 via CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release, -march=native) on an EPYC 7742 stated. Timers start after pool creation and a warmup, so the harness looks fair; gains above 50x are not capped because compiler and flags are stated.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang 21.1.7 Release (CMake preset clang-linux-release, so -O3 -DNDEBUG), -march=native, C++20; code pinned to andreasbuhr/cppcoro commit f05170fbc71aaae06dc31e32812f1caba9525377. Allocator for the cppcoro binaries is not certain: cpp/cppcoro/CMakeLists.txt links mimalloc if found, else jemalloc, and deliberately skips tcmalloc on Linux (falls back to glibc malloc), while the README's machine note says the run was linked against libtcmalloc_minimal.so.4 (which the concurrencpp, HPX and libcoro builds pick first). Baselines pinned in the suite: concurrencpp v.0.1.7, HPX v1.11.0, libcoro commit 44d12235a218a93cf6ce462f67c06a1287901c54.
corrections.caveats: Neither the repo README nor any first-party page carries timings: the README makes only qualitative design claims (the static_thread_pool schedule() will not allocate memory in the common case; async_mutex is lock-free). The numbers come from the third-party tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks suite, which measures the maintained fork https://github.com/andreasbuhr/cppcoro (its README lists only build-system, CI and header/namespace-selection changes versus upstream; no performance changes are listed), not lewissbaker/cppcoro itself. The baselines it beats (concurrencpp v.0.1.7, HPX v1.11.0, libcoro) are other coroutine runtimes, not the std::future/std::async baseline from the brief, and no std::async row exists. cppcoro loses to TBB, Taskflow, libfork, TooManyCooks and citor on the fork-join benchmarks (it roughly ties TBB on skynet: 144907 us vs 142887 us) and uses about 10x the memory of TBB or Taskflow (134 MB vs 11-14 MB); in the io_socket_st TCP ping-pong row it is the slowest of four (524717 us vs libcoro 483074 us, Boost.Cobalt 393036 us, TooManyCooks 339340 us). The author of the suite also authors TooManyCooks (a competing runtime). Allocators differ per library: the suite's cppcoro CMake prefers mimalloc, then jemalloc, and otherwise uses glibc malloc on Linux (tcmalloc disabled because it was slower for cppcoro), while the other runtimes take tcmalloc first; the README says the summary machine had tcmalloc_minimal, so which allocator cppcoro actually used is not stated. Each table cell is one process run (warmup plus timed loop) with no repetitions or variance reported. The upstream repo is dormant since 2022-09-02, and the book lead calls it unmaintained.

notes: Numbers verified against the live README of tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks. The measured code is the andreasbuhr/cppcoro fork; the orchestrator may want a repo_url note or keep the upstream id. Corrected the allocator statement (the suite does not guarantee a high-performance allocator for cppcoro on Linux).

tier_reason: tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks README shows io_socket_st libcoro 483074 us vs cppcoro 524717 us and channel libcoro_mt 409967 us vs cobalt_st_asio 910778 us exactly as claimed; code is public (cpp/libcoro/io_socket_st.cpp vs cpp/cppcoro/io_socket_st.cpp, cpp/libcoro/channel.cpp vs cpp/cobalt/channel.cpp) with Clang 21.1.7 Release, -march=native and EPYC 7742 stated. Only the io_socket_st row is a like-for-like win; the channel row compares a 64-thread pool against Boost.Cobalt on one thread.

corrections.workload: io_socket_st: TCP ping-pong of 100,000 requests over 20 connections between a single-threaded client and a single-threaded server, each on its own event loop (libcoro io_scheduler with process_tasks_inline against cppcoro io_service from the andreasbuhr fork); channel: async MPMC queue moving 10,000,000 elements with thread_count/2 producers and consumers, libcoro coro::queue on a coro::thread_pool of 64 threads (mt config) against Boost.Cobalt channel on a single thread (st_asio config; the source notes cobalt does not support multiple threads).
corrections.caveats: Weak result. The only wins are one 9% single-threaded socket row against cppcoro (itself the slowest of the four in that table) and one cross-configuration channel row (libcoro on a 64-thread pool vs Boost.Cobalt on a single thread, so not equal footing; TooManyCooks single-threaded Asio is 1.00x, 2.3x faster than cobalt, while no single-threaded libcoro channel row exists). Each table cell is one process run with no repetitions or variance reported, so the 9% socket margin is not shown to exceed run-to-run noise. On the fork-join benchmarks libcoro is the slowest runtime tested: mean ratio 2513.96x (skynet 119686148 us, nqueens 33347402 us, fib(39) 238019884 us, matmul 374412 us) against cppcoro 3.67x, with peak RSS of 14.66 GB on skynet. The brief baselines (hand-written coroutine task types, std::async/std::future) are not measured anywhere. libcoro's own README gives only server example runs without a baseline: ab TCP echo 110753.80 requests/s and wrk HTTP 200 OK 325778.99 requests/s with 2.96 ms mean latency, both on an Intel Core i7-9750H, so those are not comparisons. Repo test/bench.cpp times coroutine sync_wait, thread_pool and scheduler counters against a plain direct-call loop but publishes no results. The suite author also authors TooManyCooks (a competing runtime); allocator selection differs per library (libcoro tcmalloc first; the suite's cppcoro build skips tcmalloc on Linux and uses mimalloc, jemalloc or glibc malloc). The cppcoro rows measure the andreasbuhr/cppcoro fork.

notes: Tier A holds only for the io_socket_st row against cppcoro; the margin is 9% from a single run. Metadata checked on github.com: Apache-2.0, 968 stars, 102 forks, last commit 2026-03-31 (active), not a fork.

tier_reason: spdlog v0.16.3 README table matches the claim (1 thread 0.975s vs glog 1.066s, 10 threads 2.857s vs 3.032s, 100 threads 4.512s vs 1.139s) and the bench code is public, but the harness is asymmetric in Easylogging++'s favour: bench/easyl.conf gives it a minimal '[%datetime]: %msg' line while glog keeps its full default prefix (severity, microsecond time, thread id, file:line), and the single-thread easylogging-bench.cpp omits _ELPP_THREAD_SAFE while glog always locks. The 6-9% wins are within what that asymmetry can explain, versions and timing method are unstated, and Easylogging++ loses 4x at 100 threads.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: bench/Makefile in gabime/spdlog v0.16.3: CXX ?= g++ (version not stated), -march=native -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -std=c++11 -pthread -O3 -flto -DNDEBUG; glog linked with -lglog (version not stated); Easylogging++ included from a local checkout (-I../../easylogging/src/) with config bench/easyl.conf (FORMAT '[%datetime]: %msg', TO_FILE true, TO_STANDARD_OUTPUT false, PERFORMANCE_TRACKING false, MAX_LOG_FILE_SIZE 10485760, Log_Flush_Threshold 10485760). _ELPP_THREAD_SAFE is defined only in easylogging-bench-mt.cpp, not in the single-thread easylogging-bench.cpp. The programs contain no timer, so whole-process wall time was presumably measured externally; no run script is in the bench directory.
corrections.caveats: Evidence is a competitor's benchmark (spdlog author) from about 2015-2016, with Easylogging++ and glog versions and the g++ version unstated and the Makefile pointing at a local checkout (-I../../easylogging/src/); the bench sources use the leading-underscore macros _INITIALIZE_EASYLOGGINGPP and _ELPP_THREAD_SAFE, which current Easylogging++ spells without the underscore, so an old release was measured. Mixed result: Easylogging++ wins by 6-9% at 1 and 10 threads but loses about 4x at 100 threads. Asymmetric configuration: Easylogging++ is set to a short '[%datetime]: %msg' line, while glog writes its full default prefix (severity, date, microsecond time, thread id, file:line) on every line and no FLAGS_log_prefix change is made, so glog formats and writes more bytes per message; the single-thread Easylogging++ binary is built without _ELPP_THREAD_SAFE (no locking) while glog always takes its mutex. The 6-9% wins are small enough that these differences can account for them. The programs contain no timer, so the timed region is the whole process including logger setup, and the measurement method is not in the repo. Both libraries write to file with mostly default buffering. The project's own README says only 'Extremely fast' with no numbers, and its maintainer notes third-party benchmarks of limited setups (links g3log issue #73). That issue (https://github.com/KjellKod/g3log/issues/73, null sink, unstated units, no compiler or CPU) shows Easylogging++ 410,725 vs glog 402,970 for 1 thread string, but glog ahead at 4 threads (196,734 vs 127,895 without the option); this is directional and not used for the tier. spdlog itself is about 3x faster than either in the same table. The repository was archived by its owner on 2025-07-06 and its README recommends spdlog for new projects.
